content: 1. A gross national income (GNI) per capita of USD $12,736 or more is considered high-income. Economies are classified as lower-middle-income and upper-middle-income based on a GNI per capita threshold of USD $4,125. 2. Infection prevention and control (IPC) programs should be implemented in an integrated manner to improve outcomes and modify behaviors. These programs include tools such as bundles and checklists, which are developed by multidisciplinary teams that consider local conditions. 3. The five most common components of IPC programs include: (i) System change, which ensures the availability of appropriate infrastructure and supplies to enable good infection prevention and control practices. (ii) Education and training of healthcare workers and key stakeholders, such as managers. (iii) Monitoring of infrastructure, practices, processes, and outcomes, with data feedback provided. (iv) Workplace reminders and communication strategies. (v) Culture change within institutions or strengthening a safety climate. 4. According to WHO policy, all members of the Guidelines Development Group (GDG) were required to complete and submit a WHO Declaration of Interest form before each meeting. External reviewers and experts conducting systematic reviews were also required to submit a Declaration of Interest form. 5. The WHO secretariat reviewed and assessed each declaration. In cases of potential conflicts of interest, the reasons were presented to the GDG. If a conflict of interest was deemed significant enough to pose a risk to the guideline development process or its credibility, the experts were required to openly declare the conflict at the beginning of the Technical Consultation. 6. The WHO Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics ensured transparency by posting the biographies of potential GDG members online for at least 14 days before formal invitations were issued. Additionally, web searches were conducted to identify any significant conflicts of interest. 7. The management of declared conflicts of interest followed the WHO Guidelines for Declaration of Interests (WHO experts). Declared conflicts were considered irrelevant in all cases and did not warrant exclusion from the GDG. 8. Specific declarations of interest included: Mary-Louise McLaws disclosed that Johnson & Johnson and Deb Australia provided a grant of AUD $70,000 in 2015 for producing a video on hand hygiene. Deb also provided automated alcohol-based hand rub dispensers for a hand hygiene study in 2015. Whiteley Industries provided AUD $10,000 in 2014 for a student bursary related to hand hygiene research. GOJO provided approximately AUD $10,000 in 2012 for laboratory testing used in a research study. Several companies (e.g., Braun, Lysoform, Antiseptica, Dr. Schumacher, and Dr. Weigert) supported the German national hand hygiene campaign with approximately €60,000 between 2014 and 2015. Val Robertson disclosed receiving a research grant of USD $3,000 from the International Federation of Infection Control in 2015 and a monthly honorarium of USD $2,241 as a technical advisor to the Zimbabwe Infection Prevention and Control Project. 9. Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are among the most common adverse events in care delivery and represent a significant public health issue, impacting morbidity, mortality, and quality of life. At any given time, up to 7% of patients in developed countries and 10% in developing countries acquire at least one HAI. These infections also impose a substantial economic burden on society. 10. A large proportion of HAIs are preventable through effective IPC measures. Since the publication of the WHO Core Components for Infection Prevention and Control in 2009, the threats posed by epidemics, pandemics, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) have become increasingly evident. Effective IPC is a cornerstone of addressing these challenges. 11. The International Health Regulations (IHR) position IPC as a key strategy for managing public health threats of international concern. The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) also emphasize IPC as a contributor to safe, effective, high-quality healthcare delivery, particularly in areas related to water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) and universal health coverage. 12. The updated WHO guidelines on IPC core components aim to prevent current and future threats, strengthen health service resilience, and combat AMR. They are designed to support countries in developing national IPC protocols and AMR action plans, as well as to assist healthcare facilities in strengthening their IPC approaches. 13. The guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations on the core components of IPC programs required at the national and acute facility levels to prevent HAIs and combat AMR. They also offer guidance for adapting IPC strategies to local contexts, considering available resources and public health needs. 14. The guidelines target policymakers responsible for establishing and monitoring national IPC programs and AMR action plans, as well as facility-level administrators, safety and quality leads, regulatory bodies, academia, and civil society groups. They are relevant to both highand low-resource settings. 15. Although the guidelines focus on acute healthcare facilities, the core principles and practices of IPC are applicable to any healthcare setting, including community, primary care, and long-term care facilities. Adaptations may be necessary based on the specific context. 16. The guidelines were developed following the 2014 WHO Handbook for Guideline Development, involving six main stages: (1) Identifying primary outcomes and formulating research questions using the PICO framework. (2) Conducting systematic reviews to retrieve evidence. (3) Developing an inventory of national and regional IPC action plans. (4) Assessing and synthesizing evidence. (5) Formulating recommendations and good practice statements. (6) Writing the guidelines and planning dissemination and implementation strategies. 17. The development process involved four main groups: the WHO Guideline Steering Group, the GDG, the Systematic Reviews Expert Group, and the External Peer Review Group. The GDG included international experts in IPC, infectious diseases, public health, researchers, patient representatives, and stakeholders from six WHO regions. 18. Evidence from systematic reviews and the SIGHT group’s earlier review (1996–2012) identified key IPC components at the facility level. This evidence was updated to include literature published up to November 23, 2015. 19. Recommendations were formulated using the GRADE approach. In some cases, good practice statements were developed in the absence of direct evidence, based on strong indirect evidence supporting the net benefit of recommended actions. 20. The guidelines identify eight core components of IPC programs, six of which apply to both national and facility levels, while two are more relevant to the facility level. These components are equally important for establishing effective IPC programs and practices. 21. Successful implementation of the guidelines depends on robust strategies, adaptation to local contexts, and integration into relevant regional, national, and facility-level strategies. The support of key stakeholders and partner organizations is critical. 22. A separate resource will accompany the guidelines, providing strategies for implementation in resource-limited settings. Additionally, new IPC training packages will be developed in line with the core components and good practices.
